To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the venoms of 23 of 24 snake species tested hemolysed human red cells in the presence Ca 2+ and albumin.
the majority of the tested snake venoms hemolyses human red blood cells and that this hemolysis is correlated to the amount of membrane phospholipases in the venom.

snake venoms can cause hemolysis of human red cells in the presence or albumin and Ca(2+); that most venoms cause hemolysis by splitting phospholipids; that there is a correlation between the extent of hemolysis and the amount of fatty acid cleaved; that the amount of hemolysis correlates to the amount of phospholipase A(2) in the venom; and that the hemolytic activity is inhibited by EDTA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of hemolysis of washed red cells by snake venom phospholipases.
the mechanism of hemolysis by snake venoms.
the hemolytic action of snake venoms on washed human red blood cell membranes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hemolytic activity of a venom is a function of the phospholipase A activity and that phospholipase C is a minor hemolysin.

the hemolysis of red blood cells by snake venoms in this system is a complex process, which may be initiated by the action of a phospholipase on membrane phospholipases, followed by a protease action, and that the final hemolytic process is a combination of both.
membrane damage is a prerequisite to lysis, and the extent of lysis is a function of the extent of membrane damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
snake venom phospholipase A2 is a major factor in red cell hemolysis.
membrane phospholipase A 2 activity and hemolysis are not necessarily related.
the venoms which hydrolyse membrane phospholipides also hemolyse the red cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
snake venoms can be used to study the mechanism of hemolysis in the presence of Ca 2+ and albumin, a situation which closely resembles in vivo conditions.
snake venoms can hemolyse human red blood cells by a mechanism involving Ca 2+, albumin and phospholipid cleavage.
the presence of albumen and Ca2+ is essential to hemolysis.
